title: Rank-Transformed Dissimilarity Profiles for High-Dimensional Classification
claim: High-dimensional distance matrices show systematic within- and between-class block patterns under location or scale shifts, giving usable class signal.
layout: 4 heatmaps in a row, each with its own colorbar, ordered by shift type and strength
description: Four side-by-side R-style heatmaps of 100×100 pairwise distance matrices, with observations 1–50 in one class and 51–100 in the other. Each has a rainbow colorbar (blue = small distance, red = large) and axes ticked at 25, 50 and 75. A dark-blue diagonal runs through every panel. Panel 1 (mean difference) and panel 3 (stronger mean difference) show mostly mixed blue-green texture with horizontal and vertical stripes from individual outlying points. Panel 2 (variance difference, a=1.05) shows a warmer red-orange block for the second class. Panel 4 (stronger variance difference, a=1.15) shows clear block structure: a dark-blue lower-left block, a yellow-orange upper-right block, and cyan off-diagonal blocks. The eye goes to the last panel's strong blocks, which stand out against the noisy first three.
caption: Heatmaps of pairwise distances under mean- and variance-difference settings. Observations are ordered as $X_1,\ldots,X_{50},Y_1,\ldots,Y_{50}$. From left to right, the panels correspond to: mean difference with $(\mu_0,a)=(4,1)$, variance difference with $(\mu_0,a)=(0,1.05)$, stronger mean difference with $(\mu_0,a)=(15,1)$, and stronger variance difference with $(\mu_0,a)=(0,1.15)$.
abstract: Despite advances in representation learning, high-dimensional classification remains challenging in low-sample-size regimes, where the dominant signal may vary across applications and labeled data are often limited. We propose a dissimilarity-profiling classification framework that represents each observation by its class-wise dissimilarity profile, transforming the original feature space into a low-dimensional representation that summarizes how the observation relates to each class. The key idea is to turn an effect of the curse of dimensionality into signal: high-dimensional geometry can induce systematic within-class and between-class dissimilarity patterns under location, scale, or other distributional changes, and these patterns are captured by the class-wise profiles. Building on this representation, we introduce a rank-transformed algorithm that converts dissimilarities into class-wise rank profiles. The proposed method delivers competitive or improved performance relative to commonly used classifiers on two-class, multi-class, network, and real high-dimensional low-sample-size datasets. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we characterize the mean and covariance of a distance-based surrogate, showing how location, scale, and higher-order distributional features enter the profile representation. Contamination experiments show that the rank transformation can improve robustness. The same profile construction applies to non-Euclidean data whenever pairwise dissimilarities can be computed.
